The closest match is [Pandey et al. (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27201), a temporal-attribution benchmark covering SASRec and other sequential models. Its dual-model masking metric uses a separately trained, masking-robust probe to reduce distribution-shift artifacts in deletion evaluation. Authors report stronger faithfulness from GradientSHAP and Integrated Gradients than raw attention, with explicit analyses of popularity confounding and input corruption. [Demystifying Sequential Recommendations (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) instead searches for minimal history edits that change recommendations, providing a complementary sensitivity diagnostic.

Semantic relevance and popularity remain competing explanations. [TASTE (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.14029) reports that text matching improves sequential recommendation while reducing popularity bias; this does not establish that a particular model uses sustained semantic interests. [CoDeR (2025)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/33379) models demand shifts and distinguishes them from noise through counterfactual reasoning, but its causal interpretation depends on its modeling assumptions.

Suggested synthesis: evaluate chronological training prefixes; compare deleting recurring semantic clusters with deleting isolated interactions, matching removal count, temporal positions, and item popularity. Pair deletion with position-preserving replacement to assess perturbation artifacts. Shuffle item-to-text assignments within popularity bins, then ablate the semantic residual branch and measure paired score changes, rank changes, and top-10 retention using fixed candidates. Agreement across these controls would support component-specific model dependence; disagreement would expose recency, lexical, popularity, or distribution-shift shortcuts. These are proposed probes, not an established protocol from the cited papers, and they measure model reliance rather than causal user preferences.
